                    ### Question
                    A 40-year-old male visits a urologist and reports that for the past 2 weeks, his penis has been gradually curving to the right with associated pain during intercourse. He is able to have a normal erection and he does not recollect of any trauma to his penis. Although he is married, he admits to having unprotected sexual relationship with several females in the past year. His vitals are normal and physical examination in unremarkable except for a lesionless curved penis. It is painless to touch. Test results for sexually transmitted disease is pending. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Fibrosis of corpus cavernosa
opb. Congenital hypospadias
opc. Syphilitic chancre
opd. Fibrosis of tunica albuginea
ope. Hypertrophy of corpus cavernosa

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient's symptoms of a gradually curving penis with pain during intercourse, absence of trauma recollection, and lack of lesions are most consistent with Peyronie's disease, which is characterized by fibrosis of the tunica albuginea. This condition leads to the formation of fibrous plaques within the tunica albuginea, causing penile curvature and pain. The retrieved evidence path supports this by linking fibrosis as a manifestation of changes in the tunica albuginea. Other options such as congenital hypospadias, syphilitic chancre, and hypertrophy of the corpus cavernosa do not align with the presented symptoms or the absence of lesions. Therefore, the most likely cause is fibrosis of the tunica albuginea.
